Loss and transitions

The empty nest: when children leave home

Sadness at first is normal, but many parents find their wellbeing and relationship improve after children leave.

For two decades, life has revolved around the children. One day they pack their bags to study away, live with a partner or start working. The house falls silent and a mix of pride, sadness and strangeness appears.

The famous syndrome

People often talk about empty nest syndrome, as if it were an almost inevitable period of depression, especially for mothers. Studies qualify that idea a great deal. Sadness and nostalgia are common at first, but in most cases they pass.

What studies found

In 2008, Sara Gorchoff, Oliver John and Ravenna Helson followed a group of American women for years. Those who saw their children leave home increased their marital satisfaction. It was not that they spent more time together, but that their shared time was of better quality, with fewer interruptions and tensions.

It goes worse for people whose identity revolved almost entirely around parenting, those in a difficult relationship or those who experience the departure alongside other losses.

A nest that takes a while to empty

In Spain, young people leave home late. According to Eurostat, the average age of leaving the parental home is around 30, compared with about 26 on average in the European Union and under 22 in the Nordic countries. In addition, many return home after a break-up, losing a job or finishing their studies. For many families the "empty nest" arrives late or only partly, and adults living together need to renegotiate rules, expenses and space.

Becoming grandparents

For many people, the next stage brings grandchildren. In Spain, grandparents play an important role in childcare. A study by Bruno Arpino and Valeria Bordone using European data found that grandmothers who looked after their grandchildren had better verbal fluency, a measure of cognitive function. Caring can be a source of meaning, as long as it does not become an excessive burden or replace one's own plans.

What usually helps

  • Allow yourself to feel the sadness: it is a real farewell.
  • Change your relationship with your children, from caring for them to accompanying them as adults.
  • Pick up postponed projects: hobbies, studies, travel, friendships.
  • Rediscover your partner with new plans.
  • Do not fill the gap with control: calling every day or solving everything for them gets in the way of their independence.

References

  1. Gorchoff, S. M., John, O. P. y Helson, R. (2008). Contextualizing change in marital satisfaction during middle age: an 18-year longitudinal study. Psychological Science, 19(11), 1194–1200.
  2. Mitchell, B. A. y Lovegreen, L. D. (2009). The empty nest syndrome in midlife families: a multimethod exploration of parental gender differences and cultural dynamics. Journal of Family Issues, 30(12), 1651–1670.
  3. Eurostat (2024). Estimated average age of young people leaving the parental household by sex [yth_demo_030].
  4. Arpino, B. y Bordone, V. (2014). Does grandparenting pay off? The effect of child care on grandparents' cognitive functioning. Journal of Marriage and Family, 76(2), 337–351.
